A 23-year-old male trauma patient arrives by ambulance following a pedestrian-vehicle collision. His
primary survey shows no immediate concerns, and he maintains a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15.
Secondary examination reveals blood behind both tympanic membranes and bilateral nasal bleeding.
The patient demonstrates inability to look downward with his right eye, though pupillary light reflexes
remain intact bilaterally. His vital signs show: temperature 97.2°F (36.1°C), blood pressure 131/94
mmHg, pulse 97/min, and respiratory rate 18/min. After nasal packing controls the epistaxis, the patient
reports a new salty taste in his throat three hours into his emergency department stay. Which
complication is most likely to develop based on this new symptom? Answer Choices: (A) Orbital floor
fracture (B) Hemotympanum (C) Ageusia (D) Periorbital ecchymosis (E) Traumatic optic neuropathy
(F) Anosmia (G) Epistaxis recurrence (H) Cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea (I) Mastoid ecchymosis (J)
